articles.title_zh: Trump heads to high-stakes China summit
articles.content_orig:
Add Axios as your preferred source to

Photo illustration: Brendan Lynch. Photos: Getty Images
President Trump's trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin has the makings of an unpredictable spectacle — and that's exactly what has U.S. allies anxious.
Why it matters: Trump's stated goal for the first-ever summit between the nations' three leaders is to start a discussion on nuclear disarmament. But the fear is that he could go off script and take positions on Ukraine or Taiwan that undermine their interests  or appear to side with their chief adversaries, according to several European officials and Western diplomats.
Driving the news: Before leaving for the Philippines on Monday, Trump reiterated that his goal for the summit is to talk about denuclearization — a "tough subject," he said, "because it's very hard for any of us to say we'll get rid of our nukes, right?"
Context: Neither China nor Russia was enthusiastic about discussing denuclearization. But China agreed after Russian lobbying. And Putin saw the summit as a chance to lobby Trump on Ukraine.
Behind the scenes: The Trump-Xi-Putin summit was a topic of closed-door talks among European leaders at a meeting in Dublin last week, according to a European diplomat.
The intrigue: European diplomats said U.S. officials tried to downplay the summit and lower expectations about any substantive results.
State of play: On the same day Trump meets with Xi and Putin, his envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are expected to be in Berlin with senior officials from Ukraine, Germany, France, the UK, Italy, Poland, the EU and NATO, according to two sources.
The other side: Witkoff and Kushner also spoke on Monday with Putin's foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov about the next steps in the peace process.

articles.title_orig: Trump arrives in Shenzhen, China, where Xi Jinping’s family history runs deep
articles.title_zh: Trump arrives in Shenzhen, China, where Xi Jinping’s family history runs deep
articles.content_orig:
SHENZHEN, China — It took a trip to China for me, an American, to see U.S. President Donald Trump in person for the first time.
Trump emerged from a group of black-clad photographers and other personnel surrounding him at a welcome banquet in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Leaders' Meeting held November 17th to 19th.
Seated just a few spots to his left was Russian President Vladimir Putin who picked up a glass of red wine to join a toast led by Chinese President Xi Jinping .
"At tomorrow's Leaders' Meeting, we will discuss measures to expand mutual opening up, explore pathways to innovation-driven growth, and identify opportunities to expand practical cooperation across various fields, so as to translate more initiatives into tangible results," Xi said in Mandarin, according to a CNBC translation.
Xi was speaking broadly, but Thursday's agenda includes a bilateral meeting with Trump, and their highly anticipated trilateral meeting with Putin.
But looking at the mood in the room, it seemed that their trilateral conversation had already started Wednesday night at their long banquet table. Much of what happens at APEC, including bilateral meetings and other exchanges between leaders, takes place away from the media.
But what struck me was how little sign there was of the tension surrounding Nvidia 's CEO Jensen Huang resignation, a controversy that has gripped markets for the past 10 days.
Ahead of Trump's entrance into the banquet hall, Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao shared a friendly moment with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other members of the American delegation.
Last week, the U.S. officials said that Trump did not plan to raise allegations of Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy during his meeting with Xi.
It was a striking contrast to just two months ago, when I saw photographs of Huang and Tesla CEO Elon Musk sharing a table with Trump and Xi in Washington, D.C.
And when Trump visited Beijing in May, Huang took a few minutes to speak with reporters, including me, inside the Great Hall of the People. Musk was there too, accompanied by one of his sons.
This time, neither were visible in a room that was closely watched by the world. Musk was expected to join Trump's delegation in Shenzhen, but I did not see him Wednesday evening.
Their absence from the government-heavy banquet was striking. The world's most powerful leaders may be grappling with the implications of artificial intelligence, but they certainly didn't need the industry's biggest names at the table to do so.
China's Xi calls for removing trade and investment barriers
Putin says EU is losing industry, falling behind competition
Three things to watch as Trump, Xi and Putin meet in China
Over the months I've spent following APEC's "China Year," one thing has become clear: The forum has given Beijing an opportunity to host the U.S., Japan and other member economies at a time when unresolved tensions might otherwise have made such gatherings difficult.
But even in a year defined by talks of U.S.-China "strategic stability," the APEC events have exposed the rifts and the shifting dynamics in global power. Those dynamics were on display for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit.
Several hundred attendees, from Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun to U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue, arrived early for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit.
After waiting in silence for at least 10 minutes, the audience welcomed Xi in a distinctly modern way: by raising their smartphones to capture the moment. The applause was rather muted.
It was much the same at the more government-heavy welcome banquet that evening. So many attendees rushed to take their own photographs of Xi and other leaders entering the room that reporters' views were largely blocked.
Following Xi's morning speech, there was a lengthy intermission before Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim took the stage.
"The entire multilateral framework needs to change," he said, praising China on its "rare" recognition of smaller countries.
During the tea break that followed, attendees quickly resumed mingling. Some even brought coffee and snacks back into the room as Putin prepared to speak.
They listened as the Russian president talked about his country's economic resilience and claimed Europe was losing ground. As attendees headed to lunch, one thing stood out: Neither Trump nor any other G7 leader had taken the stage at the opening event. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke later in the afternoon.
The most visible American presence during the morning session came from business leaders appearing in a promotional video ahead of Xi's speech.
And the absence of an American voice was perhaps even more noticeable at Wednesday evening's banquet.
Trump did not follow Xi with a toast of his own. This was the same famously outspoken president, who in a winding speech in Davos, had declared that the U.S. must get Greenland .
Yet on Wednesday night in China, Trump wasn't the one holding the microphone.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow Falls as Nvidia Earnings Fail to Soothe Investors' Nerves
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow Falls as Nvidia Earnings Fail to Soothe Investors' Nerves
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia’s leadership sought to set a path forward on Tuesday’s earnings call in the wake of former CEO Jensen Huang’s departure — defying calls to re-hire him, reassuring investors that demand for Nvidia’s products remains strong, and indicating that the leadership shakeup could prompt a new or more cautious approach to key elements of the company’s business.
The company has been rocked by scandal, national security concerns and the resignation of Huang, its founder and CEO of 33 years. And leadership was under pressure to reassure nervous investors Tuesday evening, with Nvidia having lost $751 billion in market value since last Sunday.
Many lingering questions remain. But investors appeared at least somewhat mollified by the comments and earnings results: shares ticked up nearly 5% in after-hours trading following the call.
Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang’s return as CEO, tells investors ‘we’ve got this’
Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones kicked off the earnings call by saying the board does not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO, despite Huang’s statement earlier Tuesday that he would be “honored” to return should the board allow it.
Jones said the board has “every confidence” in CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress to lead the company as it searches for a permanent replacement. He added the board wants to install a permanent CEO “as quickly as possible,” but it wouldn’t rush to appoint someone until it finds “exactly the right person.”
The board is considering internal and external candidates for the role. And while Jones offered no further hints on who is under consideration, Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president and general manager of Hyperscale and High-Performance Computing, joined Kress to take analyst questions on the call — a signal of his importance as a senior leader at the company.
Jones indicated that the board is taking the national security concerns into consideration in its search.
“The board appreciates that we’re living in a world where the advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are making major changes in our marketplace,” Jones said. “Our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully.”
Why crisis at NVIDIA reverberates across the AI industry
Nvidia has played a key role in fueling the growth of the AI ecosystem by providing financing and investment to its customers to purchase its chips and build AI infrastructure.
Some industry analysts have questioned whether that will continue without Huang, who was considered the industry’s master dealmaker, even as others criticized the practice as “circular financing” that has artificially inflated the market.
Kress said on the call that the company has committed more than $100 billion to such deals as of the end of the quarter ended in October. However, she indicated that the company will carefully evaluate any deals to back would-be customers going forward.
“We remain thoughtful in how we participate and disciplined in how we commit capital,” Kress said. “We are proud of the role that we have played so far in supporting the ecosystem. As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.”
Beyond its existing deals, Nvidia will take “a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing,” she said.
The company earned $2.4 billion in sales of licensed chips to China during the third quarter — comprising just over 2% of the total revenue in its core data center business unit. But the company has ceased shipments to the country, Kress said during Tuesday’s call.
That news comes as the company faces increased scrutiny from US officials over the potential illicit transfer of its chips to China.
How the Nvidia scandal lifted the curtain on a loophole that’s giving China access to US chips
A complex network of loopholes of shell corporations and unauthorized brokers, often operating via countries like Singapore, are believed to have enabled the transfer of millions of Nvidia chips to China in violation of export controls. Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., estimated that China and Hong Kong “could comprise roughly 15%” of Nvidia’s previous revenues “when considering potential loopholes throughout Asia.”
The Commerce Department on Monday announced tighter export restrictions to prevent China from accessing sensitive, AI-powering computer chips via data centers in third-party countries.
The company is assuming no revenue from sales of licensed chips to China in the fourth quarter.
Even prior to Huang’s exit, questions were swirling about whether major tech companies might pull back on their spending on AI infrastructure as they face scrutiny from investors over when the technology will produce meaningful returns.
But Kress said demand for Nvidia’s products continues to outstrip supply, especially as a growing slate of companies and consumers seek to implement computing-intensive AI agents .
“Even in the last week, the continued ask is: How are we going to receive more and more supply to help (customers) with the demand that they have in front of them,” Kress said.
That growing demand pushed the company’s projection for full-year revenue growth in 2028 to 75%, up from its earlier projection of 70%. Nvidia also reported better-than-expected guidance for sales in the final quarter of this year.
“We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners,” following Huang’s resignation, Kress said. “They’re all 100% behind us.”

articles.title_orig: Vulcan failure caused by inadequate fuel supply to engines, ULA says
articles.title_zh: Vulcan failure caused by inadequate fuel supply to engines, ULA says
articles.content_orig:
United Launch Alliance said Wednesday that the failure of its Vulcan rocket during a launch on Sunday was caused by inadequate fuel supply.
“ULA has completed an initial integrated review of flight data from the Leo 1 launch anomaly that occurred last Sunday,” the company said in a statement . “While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines.”
The new information released by ULA confirms reporting from Ars Technica on Tuesday that the rocket’s failure was not due to the performance of the vehicle’s main engines, which are provided by Blue Origin.
This represents an important revelation from ULA and will provide some major relief to different parts of the US aerospace community, particularly Blue Origin and NASA.
That’s because the BE-4 engine is also the bedrock of Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket. This powerful rocket uses a similar but slightly more powerful version of the BE-4 engine. New Glenn experienced its own catastrophic failure in May during a ground test, a failure that was later attributed to a main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines.
After this anomaly, Blue Origin retrofitted the main oxygen valve, including for Vulcan missions. Now it’s clear that this retrofit was not implicated in the Vulcan accident. With the preliminary Vulcan investigation having largely exonerated the BE-4 engine, Blue Origin can press ahead with its return-to-flight mission with New Glenn, which could occur as soon as January.
“Following the Vulcan anomaly, Blue Origin immediately worked alongside ULA to review flight data and support the investigation,” Blue Origin said in a statement Wednesday. “Together, we identified that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines. ULA is a valued partner, and we look forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.”
Amid a worsening US launch crunch, New Glenn offers the most tangible option for near-term relief for satellite operators, including Amazon Leo, which lost dozens of satellites on Sunday. The heavy-lift rocket has many commercial and government customers lined up for launch. NASA in particular is counting on the rocket to launch a number of lunar missions in the next two years, as well as play a significant role in landing humans on the Moon later this decade.
Also a relief to NASA will be confirmation that Vulcan’s upper stage, the Centaur V, did not contribute to the failure. NASA recently contracted with ULA to use the Centaur V as its new upper stage for the Space Launch System rocket, enabling future missions to the Moon.
For ULA, however, the latest update only brings more challenges.
Vulcan represents the company’s great hope to remain relevant in a US launch industry increasingly dominated by SpaceX and newer entrants such as Blue Origin. With Vulcan on the sidelines, other companies, such as Relativity Space, Rocket Lab, and Stoke Space, could also elbow out the once all-powerful launch firm.
Although Sunday’s Vulcan flight, its fifth overall, was the first outright mission failure for the rocket, two previous launches also experienced problems. Those issues involved the nozzle of the solid rocket boosters. ULA has now spent three years trying to move the rocket out of its teething phase and into regular operations. A successful launch on Sunday could have set up at least a monthly launch cadence next year.
Now, the cash-strapped company must also contend with a new issue involving propellant management and complicated plumbing that feeds liquid oxygen and methane to the BE-4 engines. It will certainly be offline for several months.

articles.title_orig: Trump plans to meet separately with Putin on his China trip in addition to their 3-way talks with Xi
articles.title_zh: Trump plans to meet separately with Putin on his China trip in addition to their 3-way talks with Xi
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump greets as China's President Xi Jinping welcomes him after Trump steps off Air Force One at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport in Shenzhen in southern China's Guangdong Province, Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption
SHENZHEN, China — President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the U.S. status as the world's leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public.
The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the United States worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.
"It's fine," Trump pronounced on Tuesday from the Philippine capital of Manila, suggesting it was all just a consequence of being a nation that is "big and powerful."
But then the outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase and the National Security Agency's communications network began to overshadow Trump's visit. They raised the specter that artificial intelligence can disrupt daily life, as new cyber vulnerabilities identified require software to be constantly upgraded to fix flaws or other security holes, known as patching, which is supposed to improve how the technology runs.
So at the start of the second day of Trump's trip, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stepped in to reassure Americans on Trump's behalf. He told reporters there was "zero" evidence that the outages are connected or tied to rival nations, cyber hackers or criminals.
"Sometimes when you are going in to fix your system because you've identified a vulnerability, it creates a short-term disruption," said Rubio, who is also Trump's national security adviser.
Xi paid Trump a special honor by greeting him on the tarmac after Air Force One arrived in Shenzhen, China, reciprocating a gesture made by the U.S. president during Xi's state visit to Washington in September.
The two leaders greeted each other at the foot of the airplane's stairs in a handshake that became a hug as group of dancers waved flowers and flags. When Putin arrived earlier on Wednesday, Xi did not greet him at the airport despite their longstanding friendship.
Trump has signaled that he wants to take an improvised approach during his time in Shenzhen, the skyscraper-filled tech hub that is hosting world leaders for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. It's a bet that his unscripted brand of diplomacy based on personal relationships can create some kind of legacy to reshape world affairs during his final two years in the White House.
On Thursday, at a first-ever trilateral, Trump said he plans to talk with Xi and Putin about limiting nuclear weapons and bringing an end to the war in Ukraine, which began in 2022 with Russia's invasion. Analysts are not expecting substantive breakthroughs, despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting.
Before the trip, Trump's aides had told reporters that the war in Ukraine would not be on the agenda. But Trump said on Tuesday that the deaths of tens of thousands of Russian troops every month had created an opening to resolve the conflict.
"I think it's very close to getting it done," Trump said. "We're going to have a good meeting on that."
Trump also teased the possibility of a private meeting with Putin and a separate sit-down with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Rubio clarified on Wednesday that Trump was "serious" about meeting with Kim as a way of resolving tensions with North Korea. But he suggested no meeting was currently scheduled between Trump and Kim for Thursday.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., left, walks beside U.S. President Donald Trump during a welcome ceremony marking Trump's state visit to the Philippines at Malacanang Palace in Manila, Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Aaron Favila/AP hide caption
Before he landed in Shenzhen, Trump had lunch in Manila with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the Malacañang Presidential Palace.
Marcos noted that he had sent fried chicken from the Philippine chain Jollibee to the U.S. delegation for a late-night snack Tuesday and complimented Trump for "working very hard."
Trump praised the U.S. bond with the Philippines and the interior decoration of the presidential palace.
"Our people share common history, common values, common interests, common architectural tastes," Trump said. "I love what you've done here."
He said after their meeting that the two nations had reached a trade deal on Wednesday, though he had also said last year that an agreement had been reached. The U.S. trade deficit in goods with the Philippines has risen under Trump, climbing from $4.9 billion in 2024 to $12.8 billion during the first 9 months of this year, according to the Census Bureau.
There were no details about the new agreement, although the White House said it will involve Manila buying more energy and farm products.
Trump also had a short reunion with Imelda Marcos, the former first lady and mother of the Philippines' current president.
Famed for her lavish shoe collection, Imelda Marcos knew Trump decades ago through the New York City party scene. During the 1986 "People Power" uprising, her husband, Ferdinand Marcos, was ousted as the Philippines' strongman leader.
Trump called her "always the most beautiful" and the 97-year-old matriarch appeared to hand him a gift, according to a video posted by the White House.
Russian President Vladimir Putin speaks at the APEC CEO summit held ahead of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, southern China's Guangdong province on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Dmitry Azarov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin hide caption
The prospect of Trump meeting with two of America's largest geopolitical rivals has been a source of unease as the U.S. president has been less welcoming of historic allies such as Canada and NATO partners in Europe.
His tariffs that were intended to curb China's trade surplus have done little to stop the progress of the world's dominant manufacturer, which for the second straight year will have exported $1 trillion more in goods than what it imported.
Even without the digital outages in the U.S., questions about how to handle AI loom over the summit.
The technology is viewed as key to unlocking faster economic growth, but its rapid development has meant it poses national security risks and could evolve in ways that put AI beyond human control.
Trump's close tech industry ally Jensen Huang was recently removed as the CEO of Nvidia after he admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an agent of the Chinese government. Beijing has denied that she was a spy, yet the affair raised concerns about how China has been able to access Nvidia computer chips to develop its own AI models that are competing with the U.S.
When asked this week why the U.S. had not been more aggressive in cutting off China's access to advanced computer chips, Trump said there were differences of opinion inside his administration and that "We have a very good relationship with China, and you don't want to insult them."
Trump has said he does not plan to bring up Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as its own. Taiwan is the leading manufacturer of advanced computer chips, including those designed by U.S. companies.
Still, Trump expects that Xi will push him on Taiwan's sovereignty.
"I'm sure he'll raise it," Trump said. "I won't have to raise it."

articles.title_orig: Trump Says the U.S. Will “Catch” China on Rare Earths Within 10 Months - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.title_zh: Trump Says the U.S. Will “Catch” China on Rare Earths Within 10 Months - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.content_orig:
SHENZHEN, China — In a rare and surprising move, Chinese leader Xi Jinping personally greeted President Donald Trump as he arrived in China on Wednesday ahead of historic three-way talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin .
It is believed to be the first time that Xi, in power for more than a decade, has been on hand to greet any foreign leader arriving in China.
He was reciprocating the personal greeting he had received from Trump in September, when the American leader met him at the plane upon his arrival for a White House state visit . Lawmakers from both parties had criticized Trump over the move, which is also rare for U.S. presidents.
A report by Xinhua, China’s state-run news agency, said that during Trump’s arrival in the city of Shenzhen on Wednesday, Xi noted the special trip the American president and first lady Melania Trump had made to welcome him at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington.
“China is a nation that values courtesy and has a tradition of returning goodwill with goodwill,” the Xinhua report said.
After Trump descended from Air Force One, a handshake between the two leaders turned into a quick hug as rows of military regiments and performers wearing bright pink and turquoise outfits stood at attention. A martial band played the American and Chinese national anthems as dancers waved flowers, pompoms and Chinese and American flags.
Xi’s gesture Wednesday most likely reflects a desire by him and his government to “show respect to Trump,” which they know he enjoys, William Yang, a senior analyst for Northeast Asia at the International Crisis Group, said in a post on X .
“It is likely also an attempt to uphold the positive rapport between Xi and Trump ahead of a potentially turbulent period in U.S.-China relations in the coming months,” he said.
When Trump last visited China in May, he was greeted at the airport in Beijing by Vice President Han Zheng.
Putin, who has a close relationship with Xi and has met with him 50 times as of Wednesday, did not receive a personal greeting from the Chinese leader when he arrived earlier at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport. Putin was instead met by Cai Qi, a close Xi adviser and member of the Politburo Standing Committee.
Xi has met with a number of world leaders, including Putin, as they gather in Shenzhen this week for a summit of Asia-Pacific economies.
Trump, Putin and Xi are holding an unprecedented trilateral meeting Thursday on the sidelines of the summit.
Ahead of his bilateral meeting with Xi on Wednesday, Putin said he expected “great potential benefits” from the trilateral talks, which have sparked anxiety in places such as Ukraine, Iran and the Beijing-claimed island of Taiwan, where officials worry the world’s three most powerful leaders could make decisions about their futures without consulting them.
In a briefing last week, a senior U.S. official said the trilateral meeting was unlikely to produce any sort of agreement, describing it as an “entry point” and “the first conversation.”
Jennifer Jett is the Asia Digital Editor for NBC News, based in Hong Kong.
Erin Tan is a news researcher in NBC News’s Beijing bureau.

articles.title_orig: Dow slides 600 points, Nasdaq seesaws as Nvidia earnings bounce fizzles: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow slides 600 points, Nasdaq seesaws as Nvidia earnings bounce fizzles: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia shares sank around 2% Wednesday after the company issued its first earnings report since the departure of former CEO Jensen Huang .
Neoclouds bounced initially following the report before trading lower Wednesday. CoreWeave sank over 6%, Iren more than 4% and Nebius declined around 1%.
Nvidia's third-quarter revenue came in at $115.84 billion, more than $6 billion above analysts' expectations of $109.10 billion, while fourth-quarter guidance of $130 billion topped the $125.1 billion consensus, according to LSEG.
The semiconductor giant continues to navigate the fallout from Huang's resignation last week. Shortly before the results, Huang made his first public statement since resigning last week, saying that he was open to returning to the company, after an outpouring of support from prominent tech figures .
But Harvey Jones, the new and first-ever chair of Nvidia's board, said on the earnings call that the board does not intend to reinstate him as CEO.
″[Hyperscalers] are the ones that are right now feverishly looking for more focus in terms of the compute that we have available," interim CEO Colette Kress told Jim Cramer on CNBC's "Mad Money."
"This concept that anything is changing in terms of any of our types of customers — that is just not true. They are all continuing to be with us, and we have a very deep breath of different customers."
The U.S. Commerce Department announced a legal change on Monday to try and stem China's access to the most advanced Nvidia chips — which are already under export controls effectively preventing their import into the country — by restricting Chinese companies' ability to access compute remotely in overseas data centers.
Nvidia told investors in its earnings commentary that it was "not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in our outlook," in keeping with its recent language on the country.
— CNBC's Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: ‘GTA VI’ Nears $1.7 Billion In Pre-Order Sales—One Day Before Launch
articles.content_orig:
The review embargo on “Grand Theft Auto VI” has finally lifted and the game, which on Tuesday was nominated for Game of the Year ahead of its launch, is considered Rockstar Games’ latest masterpiece.
“ GTA 6 ” currently holds a score of 99 on Metacritic , which ties it with the original 1998 Nintendo 64 version of “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time” for the highest-rated video game of all time on the platform. (The recently released remake of “Ocarina of Time” for Switch 2 has a score of 96 on Metacritic and is also a 2026 Game of the Year contender.)
“Many superlatives will be heard in the discussion around ‘ Grand Theft Auto VI ‘ – biggest world, most activities, best graphics, deepest narrative – but its real triumph is the way all those features and others work in service of a cohesive, believable immersion in a criminal fantasy that is hard to grasp until you’ve played it for yourself,” Game Informer’s Matt Miller wrote in his review, which gave the game a perfect score of 10.
Thirteen years in the making , “GTA 6” is a massive open-world game that follows protagonists Jason Duval and Lucia Camino (voiced by Manni L. Perez) who find themselves stuck in the midst of a criminal conspiracy in the fictional state of Leonida after a score goes wrong.
“Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos are an interesting pair of playable characters, and unlike any leads that have come before them in the series,” Luke Reilly wrote for IGN . “Their motivations and goals are very different from the main characters of previous ‘GTA’ games, and their priority is really about escape rather than revenge or empire building. They’re not angels, and it is invariably their recklessness as small-time crooks that puts them in the wrong place at the wrong time, but the overall sliminess of their far more powerful antagonists does make the couple easy to root for throughout their story – which unfolds like four or five seasons of a prestige TV show.”
“GTA 6” officially launches Thursday in the U.S. but has begun rolling out worldwide as the clock strikes midnight on Nov. 19 in different territories, starting with New Zealand, which got access to the game Wednesday at 6 a.m. ET. While fans had been waiting to see if and when “GTA 6” reviews would drop before the game did (with several debating The Game Awards nominations being revealed before “GTA 6” was out), Rockstar Games chose to set the embargo in line with the game’s public release.
The game costs $80 for the standard edition and $100 for the ultimate version and reportedly offers approximately 80 hours of gameplay to complete its main storyline alone.
“Leonida is so lifelike that at times it beggars belief, so vast that it feels overwhelming, and outside the story missions you can do whatever you please,” The Guardian’s Keza MacDonald wrote . “There are nightclubs, gyms, flea markets, malls, restaurants, clothes shops, basketball courts, shooting ranges, aircraft hangars, projects and mansions, places to hunt and fish or go kayaking, gas stations and thousands of individuals engaged in conversation as you pass by. Interesting things are always happening in your peripheral vision. You might witness the cops chasing someone down to plant drugs on them, or overhear an interesting confrontation, or see a car speeding away and wonder where it’s going – though interesting things always seemed to happen when I was driving a stolen car at high speed towards a discerning buyer, or otherwise unable to stop and follow my nose. Thankfully, another opportunity would always present itself.”
“I have quibbles about some clunky controls and some story pacing problems in the game’s later chapters, but like crappy cupholders in a million-dollar supercar, they don’t really get in the way of what’s here. Instead, they’re minor issues to point at as I hit the gas and go 200 MPH with the radio blasting,” Kotaku’s Zack Zwiezen wrote .

articles.title_orig: Iran attacks US air base in Kuwait
articles.title_zh: Iran attacks US air base in Kuwait
articles.content_orig:
Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.
The drone attack on Kuwait was the first in more than two months. The Iranian army said it had targeted the Ali Al Salem Airbase, which hosts US forces, but Kuwaiti authorities did not report any damage.
It came after US warplanes struck an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to US military officials.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates' state oil firm said a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf waterway on Tuesday.
The recent exchanges of fire, as well as deadlock in negotiations on a peace deal, have raised fears of a major escalation in the nine-month-old war.
The conflict began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.
Since then, Iran has retaliated for US and Israeli strikes by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.
It has also attacked dozens of commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass.
On Tuesday night, Kuwait's military said its air defences engaged "drone threats" but did not report any casualties or damage.
The Kuwaiti foreign ministry condemned the attack, saying it "flagrantly violated Kuwait's sovereignty, directly threatened its security and stability, and constituted a grave breach of international law".
"The explosions seemed to be coming from far away, but hearing them again after a period of calm was both surprising and worrying," Hani Mohammed, an Egyptian resident of Kuwait, told AFP news agency.
Bahrain's military also said on Wednesday that its air defence systems had "intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks".
The island kingdom, which hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet, has reported four attacks over the past six days, following a two-month lull.
Qatar, which has mediated in the stalled indirect talks between Iran and the US, said the Iranian attacks on its neighbours were a "dangerous escalation that threatens to complicate efforts aimed at containing tensions".
The Iranian army said its drones had targeted US Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait.
Later, the army's commander-in-chief, Maj Gen Amir Hatami, warned the US and its allies that it would respond more forcefully to any new attacks on Iran.
"If the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations," he said.
On Tuesday night, US fighter jets targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm Island "with precision munitions" in response to Iranian "aggression targeting US personnel and assets", US military officials said.
Iranian media reported explosions on the island but cited a local official as saying they had caused no damage to infrastructure.
In a separate development, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) said a search-and-rescue operation was under way for a missing sailor following an attack on one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. The rest of the crew were safely evacuated and 11 were receiving medical care, it added.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre reported that a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles (24km) north of Khasab, in Oman's Musandam peninsula. It said the attack caused a fire on board that was extinguished.
Iran said two oil tankers and a ship carrying liquefied natural gas (LNG) had caught fire after hitting naval mines while sailing along an "authorised route".
At least 25 seafarers have been killed across the Middle East since the start of the war, when the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the conflict and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.
In recent months, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling through the Strait of Hormuz, allowing crude oil exports from Gulf states to reach around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts.

articles.title_orig: Mexico Leader Goes Viral in China for 21-Hour Economy Flight
articles.title_zh: Mexico Leader Goes Viral in China for 21-Hour Economy Flight
articles.content_orig:
President Claudia Sheinbaum promoted Mexico as an investment destination in an address to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) CEO Summit in Shenzhen, China, on Tuesday.
In a 13-minute speech , she also touted Plan México — the federal government’s overarching economic and industrial policy — and spoke about a range of initiatives and achievements of her two-year-old administration.
Desde Shenzhen, China, les comparto mi participación en APEC CEO Summit 2026; en representación de México, expusimos a líderes económicos y empresarios del mundo que el desarrollo con bienestar es posible. https://t.co/3AEDA9Wve3
— Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@Claudiashein) November 17, 2026
According to a Xinhua news agency article posted to a Chinese government website , the APEC CEO Summit 2026 brings together “business and political leaders from across the Asia-Pacific and beyond to discuss regional economic cooperation and future development.”
“Under the theme ‘To Prosper and Win the Future Together,’ the two-day event has attracted more than 2,000 representatives from 21 APEC economies and 13 non-APEC economies, including Britain, France, Germany and Switzerland,” the article says.
“Participants include representatives from 115 Fortune Global 500 companies, as well as heads of several international organizations and representatives of business associations from Russia, the United States and other economies.”
In addition to speaking at the APEC CEO Summit, Sheinbaum will attend the APEC Leaders’ Meeting during her visit to Shenzhen. She arrived in the southern Chinese city on Monday and is scheduled to return to Mexico on Friday.
Promoting Mexico as a destination for foreign investment, Sheinbaum touted Mexican talent as well as the country’s geographic location and its trade agreements with other nations, among other competitive advantages.
“We have engineers. We are among the top five countries in the world in terms of the number of engineers produced. We have public universities, research centers, highly educated young people and a strong industrial tradition,” she said.
“We have the capacity to participate in major global value chains, but also to innovate and build strategic industries. We have a privileged geographic location, an extensive network of trade agreements, an economy integrated into the world’s major markets, natural resources, expanding infrastructure and, above all, the human talent of a hardworking people,” Sheinbaum said.
“Mexico guarantees conditions for investment, certainty and a long-term vision for development,” she said.
As part of Plan México, the federal government is seeking to attract more foreign investment to Mexico and strengthen and support the country’s vast manufacturing sector.
Foreign direct investment in Mexico reached a record high of almost US $35 billion in the first six months of 2026 , but the pace of year-over-year growth, at 2.1%, was not particularly strong.
By speaking at the APEC CEO Summit, Sheinbaum had the opportunity to court investment from major companies in APEC economies and beyond.
Three of Mexico’s five leading sources of foreign investment in the first half of 2026 are APEC members, namely the United States, Canada and Australia. Investment from China has increased in recent years , but the East Asian economic powerhouse was not among the top investors in Mexico last year .
Insecurity, uncertainty surrounding the future of the USMCA free trade pact — which the U.S. government has so far declined to extend to 2042 — and Mexico’s controversial judicial reform, which introduced the popular election of judges , are seen as among the factors discouraging investment in Mexico.
At the start of her address, Sheinbaum highlighted that Mexico is the world’s 11th most populous country and 13th largest economy.
“But above all, we are a nation with a history stretching back thousands of years, where Spanish is spoken, but so are 68 indigenous languages,” she said.
Sheinbaum went on to say that Mexico is building its “own” economic model with “roots in our history, our cultural greatness, and the strength, talent and capabilities of our people.”
“This transformation began in 2018. And starting in 2024, with the election of Mexico’s first female president, we gave it a new dimension through Plan México,” she said.
“Plan México is a vision for the nation. It is the decision to turn our capabilities, resources, strategic position, and talent into drivers of development grounded in sovereignty and social justice,” she said.
She said that the plan is based on “five principles,” namely “shared prosperity; energy and food sovereignty; public, private, and public-private investment in infrastructure; incentives for private investment; and environmental responsibility in the face of climate change.”
Sheinbaum also said that Plan México “has a humanist vision” in which “the economy is at the service of the people” rather than the other way around.
“For decades, it was argued that the wealth of a select few had to grow first, and that over time, the benefits would trickle down to the rest of society. In Mexico, we are proving that the path can be very different,” she said.
Sheinbaum said the government and private companies are expected to invest a total of US $432 billion in infrastructure under Plan México between 2024 and 2030.
“We are transforming the country’s productive capacity, connecting regions, bringing markets closer together, improving logistics, and creating jobs,” she said.
“At the same time, we are promoting investment in industry and services through incentives, certainty, streamlined administrative procedures, and new development hubs aligned with each region’s economic strengths. This has enabled us to become the fifth-largest economy in the world in terms of foreign direct investment,” Sheinbaum said.
In her closing remarks, she said she hadn’t traveled to China “just to offer investment opportunities.”
“We came to share a vision for the future,” she said.
“A vision in which Mexico grows and, at the same time, all economies become stronger and prosperity is a shared achievement,” Sheinbaum said.
In various ways, Sheinbaum’s address at the APEC CEO Summit was similar to her annual government report ( informe ) speeches, the most recent of which she delivered on Sept. 1 . The difference was that her speech in Shenzhen on Tuesday was delivered on the world stage and was directed at international businesspeople and leaders rather than a domestic audience.
In a vast auditorium in China’s tech capital, Sheinbaum acted as cheerleader in chief for Mexico, and also for the fourth transformation (4T) political project she leads. She highlighted that since Andrés Manuel López Obrador — the founder of the 4T — became president eight years ago, Mexico’s minimum wage has increased 154% in real terms and some 17 million people have been lifted out of poverty , according to World Bank data.
Sheinbaum also spoke about Mexico’s various social programs, and declared that her government is establishing a “ verdadero estado de bienestar ” — a phrase that can be read as a “true welfare state” or, more broadly, a country that prioritizes people’s well-being.
In addition, she highlighted her government’s major investment in highway, rail, electricity, water, port and housing projects.
Sheinbaum’s speech to the APEC CEO Summit came a day before Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to address the event. Li Qingshuang , vice-chairperson of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, said on Sunday that leaders from 12 APEC economies, including Canada, Chile and South Korea, will attend the APEC CEO Summit and deliver speeches or remarks, or participate in panel discussions.

articles.content_orig:
Diehard GameCube fans can connect the controller to their original console, or use it with the Switch.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
The 8BitDo 64 was a loose remake of the Nintendo 64’s unusual triple-grip controller that did away with that gamepad’s centered analog stick. But with its new GC Bluetooth Gamepad , 8BitDo has done a much better job at staying faithful to the design of the Nintendo GameCube’s excellent controllers, including their unique button layout, thumbstick design, and shoulder buttons.
The 8BitDo GC Bluetooth Gamepad is available for preorder starting today for $49.99 in orange or purple and is expected to start shipping on December 10th. That’s much cheaper than Nintendo’s $69.99 wireless remake of the GameCube controller, although 8BitDo’s version isn’t an exact copy of the original’s shape and ergonomics. If that’s important to you, and you have your GameCube’s original accessories on hand, you can still buy 8BitDo’s $25.98 upgrade kit, which is a cheaper way to make it compatible with modern consoles and devices.
8BitDo’s GameCube redux carries forward the original’s octagonal gates around the base of each thumbstick, making it well-suited to playing fighting games like Super Smash Bros. Ultimate . And while Nintendo continues to skip modern thumbstick technologies , the 8BitDo GC features both drift-resistant TMR thumbsticks and Hall effect linear triggers.
The controller connects to all versions of the Nintendo Switch over Bluetooth, as well as PCs or handheld consoles running Windows. It also comes with a 2.4GHz wireless USB receiver for players who prefer a connection with lower latency, or you can connect it with a USB-C cable for the best possible performance.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street prepares for Anthropic IPO frenzy, despite broader AI stock slump
articles.title_zh: Wall Street prepares for Anthropic IPO frenzy, despite broader AI stock slump
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, is expected to go public Thursday in what could be the largest stock market debut of all time.
The blockbuster IPO underscores the enormous amount of money being invested in AI, and the growing influence that the technology has on everything from the stock market to the broader US economy.
The AI developer is targeting a range of $70 to $78 a share for the 825 million shares it plans to sell in its IPO. At the upper range, Anthropic would bring in as much as $64.4 billion and fetch a market valuation of up to $1.4 trillion — enormous figures for a company founded just under six years ago, reflecting the excitement around AI. The company is expected to confirm the final pricing later Wednesday.
The offering comes alongside a separate $26 billion investment from major tech companies like Nvidia, bringing the total amount raised to $90.4 billion — a figure that would surpass SpaceX’s record-setting $75 billion IPO earlier this year. That’s before additional options for banks to sell more shares, which could lift Anthropic’s total haul to $100 billion — more than SpaceX’s total $86 billion figure.
The third- and fourth-largest IPOs of all time are Saudi Aramco at $29.4 billion in 2019 and SK Hynix at $26.5 billion this year .
“SpaceX was the largest IPO in history by a wide margin, and Anthropic might be exceeding SpaceX. Both of them are much bigger than any previous IPO,” said Jay Ritter, professor emeritus and director of the IPO Initiative at the University of Florida. “What’s also remarkable is that Anthropic is less than six years old.”
The $1.4 trillion target valuation would catapult Anthropic into the ranks of the world’s 12 largest publicly traded companies. It will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ ANT .”
Anthropic was founded in 2021 when a group of employees at OpenAI left to start a new company with a focus on AI safety. That startup released its first version of Claude to the public in March 2023, a few months after OpenAI released ChatGPT to the public in November 2022.
When Anthropic released Claude Code in early 2025, it quickly gained traction with software developers. Revenue continued to soar after the launch of Claude Cowork in early 2026 and as Anthropic established itself as a core provider of agentic AI tools.
But, as a private company, there was less visibility into Anthropic’s finances. Going public means the company will now be required to disclose more information about its revenue, spending and losses every quarter, offering a pulse check on the health of the AI boom.
Your guide to the people who matter at Anthropic
The path to its public debut has not been without controversy. The Trump administration at one point barred Anthropic from releasing its advanced models to the public. Meanwhile, there are growing concerns about the potential for AI agents to go rogue and for the increasingly powerful technology to be used in harmful ways.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei spearheaded calls to “pace the frontier” of AI in September after former Anthropic employees sounded the alarm over concerns about safety at the AI lab.
Stock market strategists point to mid-October 2022 as the start of the AI bull market, which took off after ChatGPT was released on November 30, 2022. The Nasdaq Composite has gained roughly 135% since the start of the bull market, adding $26 trillion in market value. Now, one of the core AI companies is set to join the public markets.
By going public, Anthropic is in part carrying the weight of the AI boom on its shoulders. Investors are keen to see how the frontier labs can turn their models into steady profit streams, justify enormous spending on the data center buildout and deliver returns.
Anthropic expected to IPO despite market uncertainty, AI slowdown calls
Anthropic earns revenue through companies and people using its Claude products. Anthropic’s revenue has experienced dramatic growth, helping the company fetch its more than $1 trillion-expected valuation and putting it are the forefront of how AI companies are trying to become profitable businesses.
Anthropic is not profitable yet because it is still investing in its AI tools. Anthropic has spending commitments of roughly $900 billion in the coming years as it spends money to get compute power to train its cutting-edge AI models and support people using them. The company needs to lock in extraordinary revenue growth to justify its business model and valuation.
Optimistic investors believe that demand for AI tools will continue to surge as more companies adopt the technology. Analysts expect Anthropic to pursue other methods for revenue growth, including the development of specialized models that can be used in industries such as health and science.
But skeptics question whether the company can maintain its growth and revenue as competition intensifies. A bearish case for Anthropic is that AI tools are going to become more like a commodity, where customers can pick and choose between different providers with ease, making it difficult to retain strong pricing power and eating into revenue.
The IPO also comes as enthusiasm for AI stocks is cooling: The tech-focused Nasdaq Composite is down more than 10% from its record high six weeks ago.
Anthropic’s IPO could help restore confidence in the AI trade, which has been shaken in recent weeks by concerns about a slowdown to the data center buildout. But if it falls short of expectations, that could add to investors’ doubts.
“Investor sentiment toward AI has been extremely volatile, and while a successful IPO will likely turn that sentiment positive in the near term, the long-term trajectory of Anthropic’s business and performance is what could really instill greater confidence in the AI trade,” said Avery Marquez, director of investment strategies at Renaissance Capital, a provider of pre-IPO research and IPO-focused ETFs.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine Hits 2 Major Russian Refineries Again as Fuel Shortages Spread Across at Least 8 Regions
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Hits 2 Major Russian Refineries Again as Fuel Shortages Spread Across at Least 8 Regions
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Ukraine reportedly struck the Afipsky and Ilsky oil refineries in Russia’s Krasnodar Territory for the second time this month. The wider campaign has cut Russian crude processing by 30% and contributed to gasoline shortages and sales restrictions in at least eight regions.
Ukraine attacked two major oil refineries in Russia’s Krasnodar Territory overnight on Wednesday, Nov. 18, marking the second strike on both facilities this month, according to Ukrainian monitoring channels and Russian media reports.
A large-scale drone attack targeted the Seversky District of the Krasnodar Territory.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Debris from the drones sparked fires at two industrial facilities, while fragments were found at nine other locations, including private residential yards and streets, the region’s operational headquarters reported. Four people were injured and are receiving medical attention.
The Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ identified the facilities as the Afipsky and Ilsky oil refineries. Sources cited by the Russian independent outlet Astra also confirmed fires at both sites.
The Afipsky refinery is one of the three largest in the Krasnodar Territory and among the five largest in southern Russia. It can process more than 7 million tons of crude oil annually, producing gasoline, diesel fuel, jet fuel, and other petroleum products. The facility is focused exclusively on exports.
The Wednesday strike was the eighth attack on the Afipsky refinery since the beginning of the year and the second this month. It was last targeted by Ukrainian drones on Nov. 6.
The Ilsky refinery is also among the three largest in the Krasnodar Territory, with an annual crude oil processing capacity of approximately 6.6 million tons. It produces gasoline, diesel, and other petroleum products.
The facility was last targeted on Monday, when, according to Ukraine’s General Staff, three atmospheric crude distillation units were hit.
The Russian defense ministry said its air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 184 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones between 8 p.m. Moscow time on Tuesday and 8 a.m. on Wednesday.
According to the ministry, the drones were intercepted over the Belgorod and Rostov regions, Krasnodar Krai, Crimea, and the Sea of Azov.
Ukraine’s General Staff later confirmed that two oil refineries had been struck.
“Ukraine’s Defense Forces launched an aerial attack on the Ilsky and Afipsky oil refineries – two key fuel suppliers in southern Russia,” the General Staff said in a statement published on Telegram.
As per the report, explosions and smoke were observed near the Ilsky refinery, where storage tanks were hit.
Preliminary information indicates that an oil processing unit was struck at the Afipsky refinery. The facility has an annual processing capacity of 6.25 million tons, accounting for more than 2% of Russia’s total oil refining capacity.
The General Staff said the two refineries have a combined annual processing capacity of approximately 13 million tons of oil.
“Located in the south, they serve as the shortest supply route for fuel to Russian forces at the front. Therefore, every fire at these facilities means less diesel and gasoline for the Russian army, and fewer ‘oil-rubles’ – funds the Russian aggressor uses to purchase missiles and Shahed drones,” the statement said.
“Exercising their right to self-defense, as guaranteed by Article 51 of the UN Charter, Ukraine’s Defense Forces continue to take systematic measures to compel Russia to cease its armed aggression against Ukraine,” it added.
Kyiv resumed its campaign against Russian oil refineries in late October. Over the past few weeks, Ukrainian forces have struck around 10 of Russia’s 35 refineries, including facilities in Novokuibyshevsk, Ryazan, Afipsky, Saratov, Yaroslavl, Omsk, Nizhny Novgorod, Ufa, and Kirishi.
The attacks have contributed to a sharp decline in Russia’s oil refining volumes. Refineries were processing approximately 700,000 metric tons (5 million barrels) of crude oil per day at the end of October, but that figure had fallen to around 500,000 tons per day by mid-November – a reduction of about 30%, according to informed sources cited by Reuters.
The drop in refining capacity has also contributed to fuel shortages at gas stations in at least eight Russian regions, The Moscow Times reported .
Restrictions on gasoline sales have been introduced in the Leningrad, Nizhny Novgorod, Arkhangelsk, Novosibirsk, and Penza regions, as well as in the republics of Karelia and Buryatia.
In Moscow, Rosneft gas stations have reinstated purchase limits: Motorists can buy no more than 50 liters (13 gallons) of fuel per vehicle, while sales in canisters are capped at 20 liters.

articles.title_orig: I watched Trump, Xi and Putin gather in China. Here are my top takeaways
articles.title_zh: I watched Trump, Xi and Putin gather in China. Here are my top takeaways
articles.content_orig:
SHENZHEN, China — It took a trip to China for me, an American, to see U.S. President Donald Trump in person for the first time.
Trump emerged from a group of black-clad photographers and other personnel surrounding him at a welcome banquet in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Leaders' Meeting held November 17th to 19th.
Seated just a few spots to his left was Russian President Vladimir Putin who picked up a glass of red wine to join a toast led by Chinese President Xi Jinping .
"At tomorrow's Leaders' Meeting, we will discuss measures to expand mutual opening up, explore pathways to innovation-driven growth, and identify opportunities to expand practical cooperation across various fields, so as to translate more initiatives into tangible results," Xi said in Mandarin, according to a CNBC translation.
Xi was speaking broadly, but Thursday's agenda includes a bilateral meeting with Trump, and their highly anticipated trilateral meeting with Putin.
But looking at the mood in the room, it seemed that their trilateral conversation had already started Wednesday night at their long banquet table. Much of what happens at APEC, including bilateral meetings and other exchanges between leaders, takes place away from the media.
But what struck me was how little sign there was of the tension surrounding Nvidia 's CEO Jensen Huang resignation, a controversy that has gripped markets for the past 10 days.
Ahead of Trump's entrance into the banquet hall, Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao shared a friendly moment with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other members of the American delegation.
Last week, the U.S. officials said that Trump did not plan to raise allegations of Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy during his meeting with Xi.
It was a striking contrast to just two months ago, when I saw photographs of Huang and Tesla CEO Elon Musk sharing a table with Trump and Xi in Washington, D.C.
And when Trump visited Beijing in May, Huang took a few minutes to speak with reporters, including me, inside the Great Hall of the People. Musk was there too, accompanied by one of his sons.
This time, neither were visible in a room that was closely watched by the world. Musk was expected to join Trump's delegation in Shenzhen, but I did not see him Wednesday evening.
Their absence from the government-heavy banquet was striking. The world's most powerful leaders may be grappling with the implications of artificial intelligence, but they certainly didn't need the industry's biggest names at the table to do so.
China's Xi calls for removing trade and investment barriers
Putin says EU is losing industry, falling behind competition
Three things to watch as Trump, Xi and Putin meet in China
Over the months I've spent following APEC's "China Year," one thing has become clear: The forum has given Beijing an opportunity to host the U.S., Japan and other member economies at a time when unresolved tensions might otherwise have made such gatherings difficult.
But even in a year defined by talks of U.S.-China "strategic stability," the APEC events have exposed the rifts and the shifting dynamics in global power. Those dynamics were on display for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit.
Several hundred attendees, from Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun to U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue, arrived early for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit.
After waiting in silence for at least 10 minutes, the audience welcomed Xi in a distinctly modern way: by raising their smartphones to capture the moment. The applause was rather muted.
It was much the same at the more government-heavy welcome banquet that evening. So many attendees rushed to take their own photographs of Xi and other leaders entering the room that reporters' views were largely blocked.
Following Xi's morning speech, there was a lengthy intermission before Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim took the stage.
"The entire multilateral framework needs to change," he said, praising China on its "rare" recognition of smaller countries.
During the tea break that followed, attendees quickly resumed mingling. Some even brought coffee and snacks back into the room as Putin prepared to speak.
They listened as the Russian president talked about his country's economic resilience and claimed Europe was losing ground. As attendees headed to lunch, one thing stood out: Neither Trump nor any other G7 leader had taken the stage at the opening event. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke later in the afternoon.
The most visible American presence during the morning session came from business leaders appearing in a promotional video ahead of Xi's speech.
And the absence of an American voice was perhaps even more noticeable at Wednesday evening's banquet.
Trump did not follow Xi with a toast of his own. This was the same famously outspoken president, who in a winding speech in Davos, had declared that the U.S. must get Greenland .
Yet on Wednesday night in China, Trump wasn't the one holding the microphone.

articles.title_orig: Everything Kress Told Us About a Post-Huang Nvidia
articles.title_zh: Everything Kress Told Us About a Post-Huang Nvidia
articles.content_orig:
By Neha Chamaria – Nov 18, 2026 at 10:30AM EST
Everything is in place at Nvidia ( NVDA -1.55% ) on the operational and financial front. Its revenue more than doubled in the third quarter, and operating income and earnings per share hit all-time highs.
Those numbers hardly mattered this time, though. Few investors dial into a company's earnings call live. This time, it was different. The Q&A was their first chance to get answers following co-founder Jensen Huang's sudden exit.
In his first statement since, Huang said on X he'd be "honored" to return as CEO if the board wanted him back.
The board has other plans.
Chair Harvey Jones opened the Q3 earnings call and got right to the point, stating that the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." He took no questions on the resignation or the investigation.
Then he handed the call to CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress.
Kress didn't give us all of the answers, but she laid out the blueprint for a post-Huang Nvidia. Here are my biggest takeaways from the call.
"From a business perspective, it's business as usual," Kress said. "We've engaged with our customers, we've engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They're all 100% up behind us."
That answered one of the biggest questions on investors' minds: whether customers would pull back after Huang's exit. They haven't. TSMC ( TSM +0.50% ) leaders were at Nvidia's offices this week, and customers like OpenAI, Meta ( META -0.20% ) , and Amazon 's ( AMZN +3.23% ) Amazon Web Services are snapping up Vera CPUs.
Kress said Vera Rubin is off to an "extraordinary start." It brought in nearly $20 billion in its first quarter of shipments, the fastest product ramp in Nvidia's history.
As Nvidia increasingly backstops data center financing, investors have worried about circular AI-lending risks. Nvidia now carries $118 billion in guarantees, including $105 billion in credit support for a data center campus.
Kress says those guarantees apply once a project is ready. "If all of that begins and unfortunately they are delayed or they have a challenge in terms of building that, our guarantee doesn't exist anymore."
That shields Nvidia from construction risk.
"Cloud industry backlog now sits at $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion just three months ago, underscoring the significant multi-year opportunity ahead of our partners and of Nvidia," Kress said.
That backlog belongs to Nvidia's cloud customers, and much of it will turn into chip orders. Management raised FY 2028 revenue growth guidance from 70% to 75%, and expects CPU revenue to more than double in the year.
"We are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China," Kress said.
That ends a business that brought in $2.4 billion last quarter, and fresh U.S. export rules landed this week. Between those rules and analyst pressure over whether custom chips will squeeze margins, the next CEO clearly won't get a free pass.
The biggest post-founder risk is talent flight. Kress framed Nvidia's culture around the mission rather than the man. "Probably the most important thing that we think through right now is our employees," she said.
She tied Nvidia's future to its mission: "Our ambition will not change, our passion to innovate will not change, and our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change."
That was the closest thing to a reassurance, and Kress wants investors to see Nvidia's moat isn't a single visionary; it's an institutional machine already executing years ahead.
She closed the call with four words: "We have got this."
Jensen Huang built a fortress, and for now, it's running itself. Replacing a generational founder, however, is a marathon. Long-term investors should hold steady, because only time will answer some questions.

articles.title_orig: Xi, Putin blast Western 'protectionism' and sanctions as Trump lands in China
articles.title_zh: Xi, Putin blast Western 'protectionism' and sanctions as Trump lands in China
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Liz Lee, Laurie Chen and Jarrett Renshaw
SHENZHEN, China, Nov 18 (Reuters) - China's President Xi Jinping pledged on Wednesday to stand up against trade protectionism, but also gave a warm welcome to US President Donald Trump as he arrived ahead of a high-stakes trilateral meeting that will include the Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Xi greeted Trump at the airport, the first time he had done so with any visiting leader ‌since becoming president, reciprocating his counterpart's gesture at Joint Base Andrews in September when they last met.
Trump's arrival came after Xi and Putin delivered pointed speeches ahead of an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern ‌Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.
In his opening address, Xi urged support for what he called "free and open trade," trying to portray his country as a stable partner on the global stage, in contrast with the US, which has raised tariffs and taken a volatile approach to foreign policy under Trump.
In his ​speech, Putin criticised Western sanctions imposed over Russia's war in Ukraine.
At the Shenzhen airport, Xi and Trump briefly hugged and exchanged words before walking to their motorcades.
"China is a country of etiquette and has a tradition of reciprocating courtesy," Xi was quoted as saying by state news agency Xinhua. He added he was looking forward to discussing China-US relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation and the global landscape.
Trump said every meeting with Xi has been "very pleasant," Xinhua reported.
They then joined Putin and other leaders at the APEC summit venue for handshakes, a group photo and a banquet.
The three men will meet on the sidelines on Thursday and potentially discuss Russia's war with Ukraine and the US war in Iran, as well as other flashpoints such as trade, AI and nuclear weapons.
A US official, and senior Russian ‌officials quoted by Russian news agencies, said Trump would also have a one-on-one meeting ⁠with Putin. The Russian officials said no full-scale bilateral negotiations were planned.
Russia's Interfax news agency cited Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov as saying that Putin and Xi discussed the trilateral meeting. Russian news agencies also quoted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying that one hour had been allocated for the three-way meeting.
The trilateral meeting has drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the ⁠US, Britain and the Soviet Union that formalised spheres of influence, set the stage for the post-World War Two order and became shorthand for great-power deals imposed on smaller countries.
It has also unnerved some European and Asian capitals, which fear the world's greatest military powers will disregard their interests.
MESSAGE RESONATES WITH GLOBAL SOUTH
Xi's remarks came after Washington announced further restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips from companies such as Nvidia, which could further complicate a fragile trade truce with Beijing. China has pledged to retaliate.
"We must firmly uphold the rules-based multilateral trading ​system ​with the World Trade Organization at its core, support free and open trade and investment," Xi told an audience of business executives.
Western trade partners ​have criticised China for running annual trade surpluses exceeding $1 trillion through policies that support its manufacturing ‌sector at the expense of its consumers.
Beijing says its growth model is appropriate for an economy still catching up with the world's richest, but Washington, Brussels and others are concerned about China's supply chain dominance providing the country with geopolitical leverage and say its policies threaten their industries and jobs.
Xi said China will continue to invest in its industrial complex and new technologies. The world's second-largest economy will lower tariffs and further open up its markets, while standing up against protectionism and unilateralism, he added.
His "message is likely to resonate with many Global South countries and reinforces Beijing's effort to contrast its technology strategy with that of Washington," said George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group.
Trump's trip to Asia is his first since his Republican Party's defeat in midterm elections this month, while allegations involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy add to the tension.
COLD RECEPTION FOR TAKAICHI
Leaders from Australia, Canada, South Korea and others were met by dancers and soldiers hoisting rifles, but ‌Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi landed without any welcoming ceremony.
Her visit to China comes amid a rift between Beijing and Tokyo that began a ​year ago after she said Japan could deploy its military if a Chinese move on Taiwan also threatened its territory.
On Tuesday, Taiwan and Japan ​flagged incursions by Russian aircraft into their airspace.
Putin, who was speaking after Ukraine crippled the vital Kerch road bridge linking ​Crimea to Russia in a major blow to his four-year-old war, followed Xi on stage with a speech that described Western powers as "former hegemons."
He said Europe was in a "humiliating decline" and anti-Russian sanctions ‌imposed after his invasion of Ukraine had backfired.
"Experience has shown that the traditional tools of ​economic dominance and de facto coercion have largely run their course, ​having lost much of their intimidating power," Putin said.
"While sanctions, tariffs, and export restrictions may still exert a certain deterrent effect, they are incapable of halting growth—let alone crushing the economies of competitors."
In Manila, Trump vowed to deepen defence cooperation with the Philippines, amid its growing friction with Beijing over disputed features in the South China Sea. Earlier, he floated the possibility of meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China, but that has not ​been confirmed.
The Kremlin this week dismissed comparisons with the Yalta Conference as "games of political scientists," ‌but said the meeting would have a major impact on global affairs. Beijing said the trilateral will promote world peace.
Putin described the world as "turbulent" but said disagreements can be addressed by "sitting at the table."
"I therefore expect ​big potential benefit from the upcoming trilateral meeting," he said.
(Reporting by Liz Lee, Laurie Chen, Trevor Hunnicutt and Ju-Min Park in Shenzhen, Jekaterīna Golubkova in Tokyo, Farah Master in Hong Kong, and Shi Bu ​in Beijing; Writing by Marius Zaharia; editing by David Brunnstrom, Christian Schmollinger, Kate Mayberry, Saad Sayeed, Chizu Nomiyama and Sanjeev Miglani)
